label: before A20 (history); see the a20 section for the current picture
description: History of the first two rounds of work, before A20; the figures in this section are those of the tree then and are not the current ones (the current results are the tables above). Two optimisations, both in `api/app/sweep.py` and `api/app/store_pg.py`, no behaviour change (`make test` and `make test-db` pass unchanged). (1) The events the scheduler plans for one case (a breach and its first escalation rung) are appended in one transaction, `PostgresEventStore.append_many`: one row lock, one log read and replay and one commit instead of one of each per event; if the batch is refused for any reason the sweep falls back to appending one by one. (2) `run_sweep_parallel` / `shard=(k, n)`: the open cases are split into disjoint slices by a stable hash of the case id and swept by separate processes, each with its own connection pool, because replaying every case is CPU-bound Python. Measured then, single process, 100,000 open cases: 19.57 s before and 20.38 s after (the sharded route is the second change). Same machine, seed and sweep time. Timings varied by about 10% from run to run on a shared laptop.
notes: A first run, on a busy machine and before the base had moved, measured 48 s for the 100,000-case single-process sweep. It did not reproduce on the quiet reruns (17 to 26 s) and is not used here. (The unchanged tree at the start of A20, with the later milestones and coalescing in the planner, measured 47 to 61 s in one process; see A20 above.)

A17 (this branch): `POST /scheduler/sweep` now runs `run_sweep_parallel` on a long-lived pool of worker processes (`SweepPool` in `api/app/sweep.py`, used by `api/app/routers/scheduler.py`). `SWEEP_WORKERS` sets the size, default min(4, cpus); `SWEEP_WORKERS=1`, or any store that is not Postgres, keeps the single-process `run_sweep`. The pool is created on the first sweep (about a second) and kept; the rows with Workers 4 and 10 in the first table are the route itself, called in process on a warm pool, so they include the service-token check and the JSON response. Idempotency and no duplicate events across shards are asserted on the route in `api/tests/test_sweep_parallel_pg.py`, and a sweep killed part-way is covered by `api/tests/test_chaos_kill_sweep.py`.

Before A20: Is 100,000 under 5 s now met in the real route? Not reliably, and not at the default of 4 workers. Five runs on this shared 10-core laptop (other jobs running most of the time; Postgres in Docker on the same machine; the last ran with a load average of about 2), full sweep with the day's 11,276 events, then the re-sweep that emits nothing and is what the 10-second loop mostly does: 4 workers 10.46 s / 5.58 s, 7.56 s / 3.59 s, 7.11 s / 3.92 s, 7.75 s / 4.63 s; 10 workers 8.51 s / 3.36 s, 5.34 s / 2.37 s, 4.99 s / 2.37 s (met once, by 0.01 s, in the run with synchronous_commit=off described below), 10.23 s / 4.34 s; and on the quiet run 6.76 s / 3.41 s at 4 workers and 5.21 s / 2.25 s at 10 (not met by 0.21 s). Neither the single process (20 to 26 s) nor the default pool (best 6.76 s) meets the target for a sweep that appends a day's events at once; 10 workers met it once in five runs. A steady-state sweep (nothing to append) of 100,000 cases takes 2.3 to 4.3 s with 10 workers and 3.4 to 5.6 s with 4, so the 10-second loop keeps up with 100,000 open cases on a quiet machine. The shortfall is CPU, not durability: setting `synchronous_commit=off` for the workers changed the 100,000-case figures by about 5% (inside the noise) and was not adopted.

Why more workers do not scale linearly: replaying every case and appending each event is Python CPU work plus one Postgres transaction per case, and with 10 workers the Python processes, the Postgres backends and the Docker VM share 10 cores. Ideal scaling from the single-process split (read and replay about 10 s, appends about 10.6 s) would give about 2.3 s at 10 workers; the measured best is 5.0 s. Lowering the figure further needed a cheaper append and skipping cases that cannot be due; both were done in A20 (above).

a20.description: A20 added two things to `api/app/sweep.py` and `api/app/store_pg.py`; both are kept, each measured separately on a freshly seeded 100,000-case database (scenario `daily`) with the same seed, sweep time and machine. (1) The sweep index: `cases.next_due_at` (migration 012) holds the earliest instant at which the planner could plan anything for the case; it is derived from the replayed read model and written in the same transaction as every append, and the sweep selects only the cases whose due time has passed, plus those with no usable value (new cases, rows from before the migration, a changed calendar or pathway). (3) Batched writes: `PostgresEventStore.append_batches` appends the planned events of up to 100 cases in one transaction, with the per-case lock, re-read, replay and checks of `append_many`; a refused case is reported in its own slot and loses none of the others. Option (2), a cached read model per case in a JSONB column, was not built: (1) and (3) met the target. Each cell is sweep wall time / re-sweep wall time in seconds. The ablation rows switch one change off with an environment variable (`SWEEP_BATCH_CASES=1` appends one case per transaction; `SWEEP_FULL_SCAN=1` reads and replays every case), so they still maintain the column on each append. "Before" is the unchanged tree (main at 0a6ef53), run in the same half hour as the ablation rows.

rows.label: Before: full scan, one transaction per case (main)

notes: What the table says. The index removes the read and replay of the 91,196 cases that cannot be due (100,000 cases read before, 8,804 after) and makes a sweep that has nothing to do almost free (re-sweep 40.9 s to 0.04 s in one process), but alone it makes the appends slower: with one transaction per case, each append now also writes an indexed column, so the single-process sweep fell only from 60.9 s to 54.4 s (appends 48.8 s against 27.3 s). Batching alone removes the per-case round trips (appends 27.3 s to 7.8 s) but the full scan stays. Together they remove both: 8.72 s in one process, 3.93 s through the route with its default 4 workers and 3.17 s with 10, against 60.9 s, 32.0 s and 17.5 s. Run-to-run variation on this shared laptop is about 10 to 25% (the unchanged tree measured 47.3 s, 37.2 s and 21.0 s in an earlier quiet run), well inside the difference.

Cost that stays. The first sweep after migration 012 (the column is NULL) and the first after a calendar or pathway change read every case once; see "First sweep after migration 012" above (100,000 cases: 20.4 s with 4 workers, 15.9 s with 10). A sweep after a long outage appends everything that is pending whatever the index says ("Cold start" above). What remains in the 3.93 s: reading and replaying the 8,804 cases that are due, replaying them again under the lock when they are appended (the engine's safety property, not skipped), and the Postgres round trips. Option (2) would remove only the first of those; it was left out.

Safety. After every timed sweep the harness runs an untimed full scan (`full_scan=True`) and requires it to find nothing to do; a case the index wrongly skipped would show there. The same property is tested without a database over random logs (`api/tests/test_next_due.py`) and against Postgres (`api/tests/test_next_due_pg.py`).
